6.13 Monitoring and Review

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

All lessons, questions and reference answers on this site were generated by AI and have not been reviewed by a professional. Their correctness is not guaranteed. If you find an error, please report it with the link at the bottom of the page. The content is for learning only and is not investment advice.

Once an investment plan is written, it needs regular checking: the household changes, markets change, and the plan itself may be wrong. But checking too often and reacting too strongly turns into the return chasing this course warns against. This lesson discusses how to monitor and review so as to find real problems without being led by noise.

When to check

Section titled “When to check”

Monitoring can be triggered by time or by events:

  • Regularly: each quarter, see whether the allocation is outside its rebalancing bands (6.7 Asset Allocation); each year, do a full review.
  • Cash flows: when a large amount goes in or comes out, use it to adjust the allocation.
  • Life events: marriage, children, a job change, job loss, an inheritance, buying a home, a change in health, approaching retirement. These can change goals, horizons and risk capacity, and call for a fresh look at the whole plan.

A large market move is not in itself a reason to change the plan, but it can be a moment to check: that the rebalancing rules are being followed, that the emergency fund is adequate, and whether the household’s situation has changed as a result (for example a job loss).

Check C1
Which of the following should most prompt a household to re-examine its whole investment plan and IPS?
Did the fall change the household's goals, horizon or risk capacity? Or does it only call for checking rebalancing by the rules?
What does one year of a fund's performance show (6.3 Active vs. Passive Investing)? Would it change the household's plan?

The annual review

Section titled “The annual review”

An annual review checks the household’s whole finances against a fixed checklist, not just the portfolio’s return:

  1. Update the household balance sheet (6.6 The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance) and each goal’s funded ratio (6.12 Goals-Based Investing).
  2. Compare each asset class’s share with the strategic allocation, and rebalance by the rules.
  3. Check costs: the funds’ expense ratios and tracking differences, and whether cheaper equivalents exist (6.2 Fund Costs).
  4. Check taxes: whether retirement accounts are maxed, whether there are tax-loss harvesting opportunities, and whether asset location is sound (6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US)).
  5. Check protection: whether the emergency fund, insurance coverage, beneficiary designations and wills need updating.
  6. Compare actual results with the plan’s forecasts (next section), and check whether the IPS needs changing.
Check C2
In the annual review, as long as the portfolio beat its benchmark this year, the household's investment plan is in good order.
Besides portfolio returns, what else is on the review checklist? Does beating the benchmark show that funded ratios, insurance or beneficiary designations are in order?

Comparing results with forecasts

Section titled “Comparing results with forecasts”

The simulations of 4.13 Simulation and Backtesting Methods give a distribution of wealth, not a single number. A review can ask: where does the actual result fall in the forecast distribution? If results keep landing at one extreme, the assumptions may be systematically off; if they are within the normal range, a result below expectations does not show the plan was wrong.

A simple check: if the forecast for yearly returns has mean μ\muμ and standard deviation σ\sigmaσ, independent across years, then the average return over NNN years has a standard deviation of about σN\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{N}}N​σ​ (standard error), and the realized average return rˉ\bar{r}rˉ sits at about the following percentile of the forecast distribution:

N ⁣((rˉ−μ)Nσ)N\!\left(\frac{(\bar{r} - \mu)\sqrt{N}}{\sigma}\right)N(σ(rˉ−μ)N​​)
Check C3
A plan forecasts an average yearly return of 6% with 16% volatility. In the first year the actual return is only 3%. Following Figure 3-1, the most reasonable conclusion is:
One year's return has a standard deviation of 16%. How big is the gap between 3% and 6% relative to that? Look at the percentile at 1 year in the figure.
Look at the figure: with a 3% realized average over 5 years, what is the percentile? Is that rare?

When to change the IPS

Section titled “When to change the IPS”

The IPS (investment policy statement) should state when and how it may be changed. Sound reasons include: a material change in the household’s goals, horizon or risk capacity; a reasoned revision of capital market assumptions based on new data (4.11 Capital Market Assumptions); or finding a mistake in the original plan. Unsound reasons are recent returns or market sentiment.

A practical procedure: when proposing a change, write down the reason and the expected effect, wait a cooling-off period (say a month) before acting, and usually make the change modest rather than all in or all out.

Check C4
Which of the following is a sound reason to change the strategic allocation in an IPS?
Did recent returns change the household's goals, horizon or ability to bear losses? How does this differ from chasing returns?
How accurate are experts' short-term economic forecasts (4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis)? What horizon is the strategic allocation meant for?

A decision journal

Section titled “A decision journal”

A good outcome is not the same as a good decision. Investment outcomes depend heavily on luck: an unsound decision may make money by chance, and a sound one may lose by chance. Judging decisions only by outcomes reinforces mistakes that happened to work.

A decision journal records, at each important decision: the date, the information known then, the reasoning, the expected outcome and possible risks, and what would show one was wrong. At review time, the journal lets one judge whether the reasoning was sound at the time, not just how things turned out.

Check C5
A friend put half his savings into a cryptocurrency three years ago, and it has since tripled. The most reasonable way to judge this decision is:
If the same decision had lost 80% in a different case (which has happened several times, 5.5 Alternative Assets), would it still be good?
Can one outcome separate luck from skill (4.9 Performance Evaluation)?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Monitoring is triggered by regular checks, cash flows and life events; market moves by themselves are no reason to change the plan.
  • The annual review follows a checklist: balance sheet, funded ratios, allocation, costs, taxes, protection and the IPS.
  • Place actual results within the forecast distribution; their percentile depends on the size of the deviation and the length of the record.
  • Change the IPS when circumstances change materially, with written reasons and a cooling-off period.
  • A decision journal helps separate the quality of decisions from the luck of outcomes.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
Ten years ago a household's plan forecast, from capital market assumptions, an average real return of 5% a year for a 60/40 portfolio with 12% volatility. Over the 10 years the realized average real return was 1.5% a year.
(a) Roughly at what percentile of the forecast distribution is the actual result (using a standard deviation of σN\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{N}}N​σ​ for the NNN-year average)?
(b) They say: "The forecast was so far off that capital market assumptions are useless; we'll stop forecasting." Evaluate this statement. How should the review use this result?
Question 2
A household is saving for retirement in 15 years and needs 1.5 million dollars in today's purchasing power. At last year's review the portfolio was worth 800,000 dollars and 15-year TIPS yielded 2.0% real. This year the portfolio has fallen to 680,000 dollars and the real yield to 1.5% (for simplicity, still use 15 years).
(a) What was the funded ratio at each review?
(b) They say: "The portfolio is down 15%; once the market comes back we'll be fine." Evaluate this statement: what lowered the funded ratio? What does this mean for the plan?
Question 3
The annual review finds 400,000 dollars in a taxable account invested in an active large-cap fund with a 0.85% expense ratio, with 120,000 dollars of unrealized long-term gains; a comparable index fund charges 0.04%. The long-term capital gains rate is 15%.
(a) How much tax would switching to the index fund cost now? How much in fees would it save each year (thousand dollars)? Roughly how many years would it take to recover the tax (ignoring growth and discounting)?
(b) They say: "Switching costs 18,000 dollars in tax, too much; we'll just keep holding." Evaluate this statement. What else could reduce the cost of switching?
Question 4
A couple aged 58 plans to retire in 5 years; their IPS sets a strategic allocation of 60% stocks and 40% bonds. Stocks have soared for three years and the portfolio is well ahead of plan. They propose raising stocks to 80%, because "the market has done so well that our risk capacity has gone up too".
(a) If stocks then fall 40% and bonds are unchanged, how much do portfolios with 60% and 80% stocks lose?
(b) Evaluate their reason for changing the IPS. If the portfolio really is well ahead of plan, what would be a more reasonable adjustment?
